sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in the Town of East Hampton?
sections.html:
The Town of East Hampton Receiver of Taxes prepares and mails the bills, and the Assessor's Office sets the assessed values behind them. According to the receiver's page, the office handles more than 24,000 property tax bills and passes the money on to Suffolk County, the general town fund, nine fire and fire protection districts, six school districts with five associated libraries and one museum district, five lighting districts, five road improvement and water connection districts, and special use districts.

That list explains why two houses a few streets apart can carry different totals. Your bill depends on which fire, school, lighting and road districts cover your parcel. The town sits at the eastern tip of Long Island's South Shore and takes in the village of East Hampton, the hamlets of Montauk, Amagansett, Wainscott, Springs, Northwest Harbor and Napeague, and part of the village of Sag Harbor.

The Assessor's Office produces the annual assessment roll, keeps ownership records and exemption files, and maintains district maps that follow the official Suffolk County tax maps. The official Tax Receiver page is where bills can be viewed and printed, even after the collection window closes.

sections.h2: When is East Hampton property tax due, and what changes after May 31?
sections.html:
Taxes are payable to the town receiver from December 1 through May 31, in two halves. The Suffolk County Comptroller's taxpayer FAQ says the first half is due without interest through January 10, then carries 1% interest per month, while the second half is due without interest through May 31. Bills go out by mid-December, so the 2026-2027 bills are about a month away as of mid-November.

The receiver's page states that the 2025-2026 collection ended on June 1, 2026, and the online and phone payment systems closed for payments. From that point every payment, with penalties and interest, goes to the Suffolk County Comptroller at 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901, phone 631-852-3000. The page asks you to include your tax map number and contact details and suggests certified mail for proof of mailing.

  • After May 31, the Comptroller adds a 5% penalty plus interest at 1% per month counted from February 1, applied to the tax plus penalty.
  • The Comptroller's own example turns a $1,000 delinquent tax into $1,050 with the penalty and $1,102.50 if paid by June 30.
  • Taxes still unpaid on August 31 pick up a tax sale advertising fee.
  • Partial payments of at least $200 are accepted, and penalty and interest then run on the unpaid balance only.
  • Mailed payments count by the postmark date. A metered postmark does not count.

A missing bill does not excuse a late payment. The Comptroller states that the owner stays liable for penalties and interest even if the bill never arrived, so ask the receiver for a duplicate if yours is missing.

sections.h2: How do I challenge my East Hampton assessment?
sections.html:
File a complaint on form RP-524 with the town assessor during the grievance period, which runs from May 1 through Grievance Day on the third Tuesday in May. In 2026 that day was May 19. In 2027 the third Tuesday falls on May 18.

The Assessor's Office page lays out the yearly cycle for East Hampton:

  • July 1 of the prior year is the valuation date.
  • March 1 is the taxable status date, and new exemption applications and renewals are due by then.
  • May 1 is when the tentative roll opens for public viewing and the grievance period starts.
  • July 1 is the final roll for the current year.
  • The Suffolk small claims assessment review (SCAR) deadline in 2026 was July 31, and the town's forms page says it must be filed 30 days after the final roll closes.

The town does not accept grievance or exemption applications by email or fax. If you want proof that your grievance arrived, send it return receipt. The forms page also carries a plain-language booklet called What to Do if You Disagree With Your Assessment.

sections.h2: What do the numbers say about homes in East Hampton?
sections.html:
East Hampton is mostly owner-occupied, and the median home value is over a million dollars. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts page for the town lists the figures below.

sections.h2: Does STAR still lower school tax for East Hampton homeowners?
sections.html:
Yes, through the STAR credit. The state's STAR eligibility page says the credit arrives as a check or direct deposit that you use toward school taxes, while the older exemption on the bill continues only for people who have received it since 2015 on the same primary residence. The exemption is no longer available to new homeowners.

The East Hampton assessor's page tells new Basic and Enhanced STAR applicants to register with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance. The state's Types of STAR page gives the Basic credit an income limit of $500,000 and sets Enhanced STAR, for owners aged 65 and over, at $110,750 or less for the 2026-2027 school year. STAR applies to school district taxes only.

To qualify for a credit in a given year, the owner must own the property and live in it as the primary residence as of July 1 of that year. A buyer who closes after that date registers for the following year.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid tax when I sell an East Hampton house?
sections.html:
Unpaid tax follows the property, so it has to be paid or settled when the title changes hands. The Comptroller's FAQ explains the sequence: if taxes are still unpaid at the tax lien sale, usually held in December, the Comptroller sells a lien to Suffolk County to cover the delinquent tax for that year.

The owner or anyone with an interest can redeem within twelve months of the sale date. Property assessed as a one, two or three-family residence gets thirty-six months. If the redemption period lapses, the county issues a tax deed, and an application to redeem after that goes to the Department of Planning, Division of Real Estate.

  1. Pull your current bill from the receiver's portal to see what is paid for the 2026-2027 year once bills are out.
  2. If anything from an earlier year is open, call the Comptroller at 631-852-3000 for a payoff figure that includes penalty and interest.
  3. Give the payoff figure to the closing attorney or title company so it can be settled at the closing.
  4. Tell the buyer to contact the receiver for a current bill, since the Comptroller advises new owners to do exactly that.

If the house is also being sold as-is, the payoff figure is one more item on the closing statement, and the receiver and Comptroller are the two offices that can supply it.

faqs.q: When is the first half of East Hampton property tax due?
faqs.a: Through January 10 without interest, according to the Suffolk County Comptroller. After that date the first half carries 1% interest per month until May 31. The second half can be paid without interest through May 31.

faqs.q: Where do I pay East Hampton tax after May 31?
faqs.a: To the Suffolk County Comptroller, 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901, phone 631-852-3000. The town receiver's page says the online and phone systems close for payments once collection ends, so include your tax map number and use certified mail if you pay by post.

faqs.q: Will the town waive the penalty if I never received my bill?
faqs.a: No. The Comptroller states that the taxpayer is responsible for tax on property they own, and that a bill that never arrived does not remove penalties or interest. Ask the receiver for a duplicate bill as soon as you notice it is missing.

faqs.q: What is the last day to grieve an East Hampton assessment?
faqs.a: The third Tuesday in May, which was May 19 in 2026 and is May 18 in 2027. The grievance period opens May 1 when the tentative roll is available. Applications are not accepted by email or fax.

faqs.q: Can I sell my East Hampton house while the county holds a tax lien on it?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the lien is settled at or before closing. Suffolk allows redemption within twelve months of the lien sale, or thirty-six months for a one to three family home. Ask the Comptroller for the payoff amount and hand it to the closing attorney or title company.
